findings.title: The [020] deferral is correct, but its stated premise is false — and the one genuinely new path it misses is safe only by a zero-margin accident of Decision 1
findings.description:
The spec (Solution, and the last row of Risks) justifies deferring tech debt [020] with: "tables and indexes become the first screens with a non-empty DiffIntvl whose width is version-dependent, so [020] becomes reachable on a diffed screen where it previously could not be." Both halves were checked against the code and both are wrong.

(a) It overstates. [020]'s malformed-archive class is ALREADY fully reachable on these two screens today. `internal/view/view.go:88,99` seeds `tables` with `DiffIntvl {1,18}` and `indexes` with `{1,5}` — non-empty before this feature. `stat.NewPGresultFile` json.Unmarshals `Ncols` straight out of the archive, and `PGresult.validate` (internal/stat/postgres.go:559) compares each row against `len(r.Cols)` and `Nrows` against `len(r.Values)` — never `Ncols` against `len(Cols)`. `diff()` then walks `for l := 0; l < curr.Ncols; l++` and indexes `curr.Values[i][l]`. An archive declaring `Ncols: 999` over a real `tables` sample panics `pgcenter report -t` on today's develop. Version-dependence has nothing to do with it. The feature does not widen this class at all.

(b) It understates, by missing the one path that IS new. `report.go:276` gates the prev-snapshot drop on `prevMeta.version != d.meta.version` — the POSTGRES version. `record -a` (record/recorder.go:64, `AppendFile`) appends into an existing tar, and nothing in the archive records the pgcenter version. So recording `tables` on a PG 19 server with pgcenter 0.11 (19 columns), upgrading pgcenter, and appending with 0.12 (20 columns) produces two same-PG-version samples of different width, `versionChanged` is false, and `diff(curr, prev)` runs across the boundary. That shape cannot exist for `tables`/`indexes` today because their width is constant; after this feature it can, from ordinary user actions and a well-formed archive.

It does not panic — and the reason is Decision 1, with exactly zero margin. `diff`'s interval test is inclusive (`if l < interval[0] || l > interval[1]` skips), so the highest index handed to `prev.Values[j][l]` is `DiffIntvl[1]`. For `tables` that is 18, and the PG<=18 layout has 19 columns (indices 0..18) — the last valid index. For `indexes` it is 5 against 6 columns — again the last valid index. Appending `stats_age` at the tail is the only thing keeping `DiffIntvl[1]` inside the narrower row. Had Decision 1 gone the ADR [012] way (mid-layout insertion, version-dependent `DiffIntvl`), this ordinary archive would dereference past the end of `prev.Values[j]`.

So the deferral is defensible — more strongly than the spec argues — but the property it now depends on is stated nowhere and asserted by no test. Decision 1's rationale is entirely about readability and about ADR [012]'s silent-wrong-diff hazard; it never mentions that the tail placement is also what keeps the diff loop in bounds. The next feature that adds a column to `tables` or `indexes` will weigh mid-layout insertion against readability with no record of the crash consequence.
findings.location: Section: Solution (para 2); Decision 1; Decision 8; Risks (last row) — against internal/stat/postgres.go:559 (validate), :606-660 (diff), report/report.go:276-320, record/recorder.go:64
findings.impact: Two effects. First, the tech-debt register is left describing [020]'s reachability incorrectly, so the next reviewer weighing whether to close it works from a wrong map — it is already reachable on eight diffed screens including these two, not newly reachable here. Second, and materially: an undocumented, untested invariant (DiffIntvl[1] < min(Ncols) across the selector's versions) now stands between an ordinary `record -a` archive spanning a pgcenter upgrade and an index-out-of-range panic in diff(). Nothing signals its violation; a future mid-layout column insertion on these screens would introduce a crash reachable without any malformed input.

findings.title: The "no special privileges (measured)" claim for the new view is verified only as superuser, against the project's own established convention
findings.description:
Question 5 checks out at the design level — nothing in the feature reads a restricted catalog, calls a privileged function, or branches on role membership. `pg_stat_all_tables` is unrestricted, the join needs no ACL, and the view carries no `ExtPGSSSchema`-style guard because it needs none.

The gap is in how the claim is held. Every integration test connects through `postgres.NewTestConnectVersion`, which hardcodes user `postgres` (internal/postgres/testing.go:50) against a `trust` pg_hba (testing/prepare-test-environment.sh) — i.e. superuser. The claim was measured by hand on a stand as superuser and nothing in the Testing Strategy re-measures it.

This is not a generic "you should test as an unprivileged user" remark. The project already does exactly that, and did it for the immediately preceding feature: `internal/query/archiver_test.go:212,250` drives the archiver query twice, once through `postgres.SetupTestRole(conn, archiverRoleMonitor, true)` and once through `SetupTestRole(conn, archiverRoleNoRole, false)`, precisely because 017's privilege assumption needed to be a test rather than a note. `overview_test.go:193,227` does the same. Feature 018 introduces a brand-new PG 19 catalog view whose GA-time ACL is not yet settled, and skips the pattern.

The Risks table compounds it: it bets on "locked column-name test on the new query" to catch beta-to-GA drift. That test asserts names and order of a result set fetched as superuser. A GA that puts `pg_stat_autovacuum_scores` behind `pg_monitor` — a plausible outcome for a view exposing per-relation autovacuum internals — changes no column name and reddens nothing. The drift guard is blind to the exact axis that is most likely to move.
findings.location: Section: Testing Strategy > Integration tests; Section: Risks (row 1); Task 1 — against internal/postgres/testing.go:50, internal/query/archiver_test.go:212-250
findings.impact: If PG 19 GA restricts the view, or restricts any column of it, the screen fails for every non-superuser connection while the whole CI matrix stays green. The user-visible symptom is the generic query error in place of the table, on a screen the `t` cycle now reaches by reflex, with no hint that the cause is privileges rather than version. It ships as a user report instead of a red test.

findings.title: The wraparound fixture mutates the shared CI cluster irreversibly, with no cleanup, no autovacuum suppression, and a count assertion on shared state
findings.description:
The fixture (Testing Strategy > Integration tests; interview notes 28-30) does three things to the shared PG 19 cluster on port 21919, in the shared `pgcenter_fixtures` database: creates `toast_probe`, sets `toast.autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 100000` on it, and calls a procedure that commits ~120000 separate transactions. The spec specifies none of the surrounding hygiene.

1. **No cleanup is declared.** Nothing drops `toast_probe` or resets the reloption. `prepare-test-environment.sh` builds these clusters once and every package runs against them for the life of the container. MEMORY.md documents a local workflow where the developer re-runs `make test` against a persistent container, so the table and its lowered freeze horizon accumulate across runs on the developer's machine, not just in a throwaway CI container.

2. **No `autovacuum_enabled = false` on the probe.** `for_wraparound` is true exactly while `age(relfrozenxid)` exceeds the (now 100000) horizon. Autovacuum sees that within one `autovacuum_naptime` (60s default — nothing in the fixture config changes it), launches an anti-wraparound vacuum on the toast table, advances `relfrozenxid`, and the flag clears. The assertion the whole fixture exists to make is therefore live for a bounded window after `burn()` returns. That window is not stated, not enforced, and not defended against a slow runner or a reordered test. It also undermines the acceptance criterion that the mutation (deleting `OR s.for_wraparound`) must be observed red on the named assertion — a green-when-it-should-be-red run and a flag-already-cleared run are indistinguishable.

3. **The assertion is a count over shared state.** Interview note 30 pins the discriminating check as "user mode without the escape hatch = 1 row, with it = 2". `go test ./...` runs packages concurrently by default, and every package points at the same six clusters. A leftover `toast_probe` from a previous run, or a second fixture flagged concurrently, moves that count. The repo already knows this hazard: internal/stat/postgres_test.go:241 carries a comment about two packages racing on a cluster-global role.

4. **The XID burn is irreversible.** 120000 XIDs per run against a 2e9 budget is not a wraparound risk (~16000 runs), but it is monotonic, it moves `age(datfrozenxid)` for every other test on that cluster, and the anti-wraparound vacuum it provokes takes a ShareUpdateExclusiveLock that will not yield to a lock waiter — a concurrent test doing DDL on that relation blocks until it finishes rather than being let through.

The roadmap owner's stated principle for this feature was to keep the blast radius inside the feature's own area (Decision 8). The fixture is the one place where the feature reaches outside it, and it is the one place the spec does not bound.
findings.location: Section: Testing Strategy > Integration tests (the for_wraparound escape hatch bullet); Section: Risks (row 2); Task 1 — against testing/prepare-test-environment.sh, testing/fixtures.sql, internal/postgres/testing.go:50
findings.impact: On a shared cluster: a permanently lowered freeze horizon on a table that no test owns after the run ends, repeated anti-wraparound vacuum activity, and monotonic XID consumption visible to every other package. On test integrity, which is the sharper cost: a discriminating assertion whose truth expires on a 60-second timer and whose expected value is a row count over state other tests and previous runs can move. Both failure modes present as flakiness, and flakiness on a mutation-verified assertion trains reviewers to re-run — which is exactly how the 18 unfallible tests of feature 017 got through.
findings.recommendation:
Bound the fixture inside Task 1:
1. Create the probe with autovacuum disabled so the flag cannot be cleared underneath the assertion, and only then burn:
```sql
CREATE TABLE toast_probe_018 (id int, payload text);
ALTER TABLE toast_probe_018 SET (
    toast.autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 100000,
    toast.autovacuum_enabled = false   -- keep the flag up for the assertion's lifetime
);
```
2. Give it a feature-unique name (`toast_probe_018`) and `t.Cleanup(func(){ DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ... })` so a re-run against a persistent container starts from a known state and a failed run does not poison the next one.
3. Make the assertion existence-based rather than count-based — `require.Contains(rows, "pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>")` resolved from the probe's `reltoastrelid` — so a leftover or concurrent fixture cannot move it. The discriminating property (present with the escape hatch, absent without it) survives the change; the fragility does not.
4. Guard the test with `t.Parallel()` omitted and a note that it is the only test in the suite that mutates cluster-wide XID state, so it is not casually parallelised later.
5. State the residual in the spec: ~120k XIDs per run are irreversible even with cleanup.

findings.title: Template construction introduces no injection surface — ViewType is a two-valued internal toggle, and the new query is the first that does not splice it
findings.description:
Verified end to end, as asked. `query.Options.ViewType` is written in exactly two places: `NewOptions` seeds it to the literal `"user"` (internal/query/query.go:47), and `toggleSysTables` flips it between the literals `"user"` and `"all"` (top/config_view.go:458-462). No CLI flag, no config file, no dialog, and no report path assigns it. `query.Format` is a plain `text/template` with no `Funcs()`, so `ne` is the builtin comparison and `{{if ne .ViewType "all"}}` cannot execute anything.

The new query is in fact strictly safer than its neighbours: `tables.go:19`, `indexes.go:10` and `sizes.go:17` splice `{{.ViewType}}` into a relation name (`pg_stat_{{.ViewType}}_tables`), which is a genuine string-into-SQL sink held safe only by the two-literal domain. The new query never splices the value — it only compares it — so it adds zero splice sites while adding a screen.

One observation rather than a defect: Task 2 duplicates each of `tables.go` and `indexes.go` into a `...PG19` constant, and the copy carries the `{{.ViewType}}` splice with it. That takes the codebase from three splice sites to five. Nothing about the feature widens ViewType's domain, so this is not exploitable — but the invariant that keeps five SQL-building sites safe lives entirely in a two-branch if-statement in top/config_view.go with no assertion anywhere.
findings.location: internal/query/query.go:30,47; top/config_view.go:458-462; Task 2 (new PG19 constants in internal/query/tables.go, internal/query/indexes.go)
findings.impact: None today. The note is defence in depth: five queries build a relation name from a package-level string field whose safety rests on convention at a single call site, and the feature adds two of the five.

findings.title: Tech debt [029] is not widened by this feature — the new screen is a third surface of an existing class, and should be listed as such rather than re-argued
findings.description:
Checked as asked. `top/stat.go:1222` (`printDataCell`) still writes row values with no SGR wrapper and no escape stripping, so a crafted `relname` reaches the terminal. The new screen renders `relation` as `schemaname || '.' || relname` — byte-for-byte the same construction and the same source as `tables.go:5` and `sizes.go`, which already render it. The remaining ten columns are numerics rounded to 2 decimals and three booleans emitted through `::text`, none of which can carry a payload.

Nothing about the feature lengthens the exposure window either. `autovacuum_scores` carries `DiffIntvl {0,0}` and `NotRecordable: true`, so it adds no diff path, no archive sink, and no new persistent buffer. [029]'s two recorded aggravating factors are untouched: the pause-freeze extension from 016 applies to this screen exactly as it applies to `tables`, and the logtail buffer is not involved.

One nuance worth naming, because it is the only behavioural change on this axis: the `for_wraparound` escape hatch (Decision 4) makes system-schema relations visible in `user` mode. Those names are catalog-generated (`pg_toast.pg_toast_16532`) and not attacker-influenceable, and the `,` toggle already shows the same rows in `all` mode, so the escape hatch does not reach any name a user could not already display.

Conclusion: no widening. Recording it so the answer is a checked result rather than an assumption.
findings.impact: None beyond the already-registered [029]. The surface grows by one screen displaying values of a kind two existing screens already display.
findings.recommendation: In Task 7, when [020] and [035] are updated, add one line to [029] listing `autovacuum_scores` alongside `tables`/`sizes` as a screen that renders server-controlled relation names. Do not re-argue the decision — the asymmetry between the sanitised cmdline and the unsanitised stats table is already recorded and unchanged. No code change.

findings.title: Reporting an archive appended across a pgcenter upgrade will fail with "zero or negative width, skip" once tables/indexes have two layouts
findings.description:
Consequence of the same same-PG-version width change described in the first finding, on the render path rather than the diff path. `formatStatSample` (report/report.go) latches `view.Aligned` on the first sample and only `versionChanged` lowers it (report.go:297-300). A tar whose earlier `tables` samples were recorded by pgcenter 0.11 (19 columns) and whose appended samples come from 0.12 (20 columns) reports the same `meta.version`, so the latch is never lowered: `view.ColsWidth` holds keys 0..18, the 20-column sample is rendered, and `printStatSample` reads `view.ColsWidth[19]` out of a map as 0 and returns `fmt.Errorf("zero or negative width, skip")` (report/report.go:624).

The outcome is an error, not a panic and not a hang — [021] restored the zero-width guard and [026] added the `dataCh` drain, so `doReport` unwinds and prints. But the message names no column, no sample and no cause, and per active tech debt [034] the process still exits 0, so a wrapper script sees an empty report and a success code.

This is the pre-existing [035]/[021] shape rather than new code, and it is only reachable once a screen has two layouts under one PG version — which is what this feature gives `tables` and `indexes`. The version-change path itself is correctly handled; this is specifically the pgcenter-version boundary that `versionChanged` cannot see.
findings.location: report/report.go:276-300 (version-change branch), report/report.go:616-630 (printStatSample width guard); Section: Backward Compatibility > Consumer impact
findings.impact: A user who upgrades pgcenter and keeps appending to an existing archive with `record -a` gets an unreportable file for the tables/indexes screens, with a message that does not point at the cause. Combined with [034]'s exit code 0, a scripted report writes an empty file and reports success.
findings.recommendation:
No code change inside this feature — the fix belongs with [035]/[021] in the shared alignment path, and Decision 8's scope boundary is the right call. Two documentation items instead:
1. Correct the Backward Compatibility claim. It currently reads "Recorded archives: unaffected ... old archives replay exactly as before", which is true for a homogeneous archive and false for one appended across a pgcenter upgrade. State the exception.
2. Note it in `doc/release-notes/v0.12.0.md` under Task 7, with the workaround (report the pre-upgrade and post-upgrade archives separately, or start a fresh file after upgrading). Recording the pgcenter version in `meta.*` so `report` can drop the previous snapshot on a binary-version change is the eventual fix and belongs in the tech-debt register next to [035], not in this feature.
